title: Network isolation and day-2 operations for private deployments
author: Mei Chen
content:
Summary

This document describes recommended network isolation patterns, hardware/network prerequisites, and Day-2 operational procedures for Redwood private deployments (VPC and on-prem variants). It is written for SREs, platform engineers, and solutions architects responsible for deploying and operating Redwood Private in customer-controlled networks.

Key goals
- Provide repeatable, secure network topologies for tenant isolation and egress control.
- Give a compact Day-2 playbook for monitoring, upgrades, and rollback with minimal customer downtime.
- Define a baseline customer hardware/network checklist and suggested observability/alert thresholds.

Scope & audience
- Applies to Redwood Private installations using: dedicated VPC deployments (customer-managed VPC and subnets) and fully on-prem clusters (air-gapped or connected).
- Not a step-by-step installer: see deployment-specific install guides. This doc focuses on operational policies, network isolation patterns, and upgrade/rollback runbooks.

High-level recommendations (TL;DR)
1) Use minimal blast-radius network segments: control-plane, compute-inference, storage/metrics, and admin.
2) Prefer eBPF/NetworkPolicy-based enforcement inside cluster + perimeter firewall for cross-segment egress.
3) Always verify KV-cache and persistent volumes are drained before rolling inferred-model-serving pods.
4) Maintain a one-window rolling upgrade with canary traffic routing and automatic fallback.

Reference topologies
1. Per-tenant VPC segmentation (recommended for multi-tenant customers)
- Each tenant is assigned a dedicated subnet and security group.
- Shared control plane is placed in a separate management VPC and peered (transit gateway or VPC peering) with tenant VPCs.
- Inference compute lives in tenant subnets behind a private ALB/NLB.

2. Single-tenant VPC with internal isolation (recommended for enterprise customers)
- One VPC containing multiple subnets: control (management), inference (GPU-backed), storage, and tooling.
- Network ACLs and security groups enforce service-to-service connectivity. Internal Kubernetes NetworkPolicies provide pod-level restrictions.

3. Air-gapped on-prem (recommended for highest regulation)
- Control plane can be deployed as a customer-managed, isolated control API appliance with an admin bastion.
- All artifact repositories, model registries, and metrics backends are local; outbound egress is strictly controlled.

Design patterns and controls
- Segmentation layers: perimeter (firewall/TGW), VPC/subnet, Kubernetes namespace, pod NetworkPolicy.
- Default-deny egress inside the cluster; explicit egress for metrics (Prometheus push/remote write) and logging endpoints.
- Use mutual TLS for service-to-service calls (mTLS) where supported.
- Leverage host-based eBPF policies for fine-grained process-level controls when available.

Baseline hardware & network requirements (customer checklist)
| Component | Minimum | Recommended | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| GPU nodes | 1 x A10 / A30 equivalent | 8 x A100 (40GB) | For proof-of-concept vs production throughput sizing |
| CPU nodes (control/infra) | 4 cores, 16GB | 8 cores, 32GB | etcd and control plane needs stable CPU \n| Disk | 200GB SSD | 2 x 1TB NVMe RAID1 | Models/cache store on local NVMe for performance |
| Network | 1 Gbps | 10 Gbps (RDMA encouraged) | Low jitter required for KV cache and data transfers |
| Internal MTU | 1500 | 9000 | Jumbo frames recommended for GPU clusters |
| Control plane availability | N+2 | N+3/HA | 3 control-plane replicas minimum\n
(Adapt numbers to expected concurrency/throughput; Redwood solutions engineering can assist with capacity planning.)

Day-2 operations checklist (run-before and run-during)
Pre-shift (daily)
- Verify control-plane health: kubectl get componentstatuses, etcd metrics, API server latencies.
- Check node GPU utilization and memory pressure.
- Ensure KV-cache hit ratio, cache size, and eviction rate within expected ranges.
- Confirm backups: model registry snapshot timestamp within SLA.

Runbook: common operational tasks
1) Rotate TLS certs (internal control plane)
- Step 1: Notify teams and pause non-critical scheduled jobs.
- Step 2: Stage new certs to secret store (customer KMS) and update deployment: kubectl apply -f control-plane-certs.yaml
- Step 3: Rolling restart of control-plane pods with readiness probes; verify clients reconnect.

2) Evacuate a GPU node (pre-upgrade or pre-failure)
- Run: kubectl cordon <node>
- Evict inference pods gracefully: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --timeout=30m
- Confirm KV-cache persisted to persistent volume or fallback cache. If cache is ephemeral for model serving, warm new nodes with prefix cache prefetch (see cache-warmup snippet).

3) Cache warmup (example)
- Purpose: reduce first-request latency when new nodes come online.
- Example curl-based warmup for a model route (replace placeholders):
  for prompt in $(cat warmup-prompts.txt); do \
    curl -s -X POST \\ \
      -H 'Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY' \\ \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \\ \
      --data '{"model":"gpt-x","prompt":"'$prompt'","max_tokens":16}' \\ \
      https://internal-api.example.local/v1/generate; \
  done

Upgrade and rollback procedure (control-plane and runtime)
Principles:
- Canary -> staged rollout -> global -> verification; automatic fallback within defined timeout.
- Preserve prompts, model cache, and persistent volume attachments on nodes.

Control-plane upgrade (recommended window: low-traffic 2–4 hours)
1. Create canary namespace: apply release image to 1 control-plane replica or dedicated canary cluster.
2. Smoke test APIs (generation, chat, embeddings) against canary.
3. If smoke tests pass, schedule phased rollout: 25% -> 50% -> 100% control-plane pods. Use rolling update strategy with maxUnavailable=1.
4. Monitor telemetry: API latency (p50/p95/p99), request error rate, Kubernetes restart rate.
5. If errors > thresholds (see Alerts section) revert to previous image: kubectl rollout undo deployment/control-plane --to-revision=<rev>.

Runtime (inference) upgrade
1. Pre-stage new runtime image in an isolated pool.
2. Route 5–10% of traffic to the new pool (traffic-splitting via internal LB or service mesh weight).
3. Run full eval suite against that pool using production prompts.
4. If regressions detected, scale down new pool and re-route; otherwise gradually increase weight.
5. To rollback: remove new pool from LB and scale previous image back up; ensure KV cache compatibility.

Rollback safety notes
- Always maintain compatible model-served artifact versions across runtime variants; keep a 24–48 hour window where both binaries can co-exist.
- Preserve PV snapshots before runtime with potential data migrations.

Alerting & SLOs (suggested thresholds)
- API request p95 latency: 200ms (chat short prompts), alert if > 350ms sustained for 5m.
- Request error rate: alert at > 0.5% sustained over 1m or > 1% over 5m.
- GPU OOM events: alert on first occurrence; treat as P1.
- Control plane API failures: alert at > 3 failures/minute or > 5% error budget burn in 1 hour.

Example automation snippets
Terraform: minimal security group for inference nodes\
```
resource "aws_security_group" "inference" {
  name = "redwood-inference-sg"
  vpc_id = var.vpc_id

  ingress {
    from_port = 443
    to_port   = 443
    protocol  = "tcp"
    cidr_blocks = [var.internal_lb_cidr]
  }

  egress {
    from_port = 0
    to_port = 0
    protocol = "-1"
    cidr_blocks = ["10.0.0.0/8"]
  }
}
```

Kubernetes NetworkPolicy (deny-by-default example)
```
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny
  namespace: inference
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
```

Troubleshooting matrix (quick reference)
- Symptom: Control-plane unreachable for a subset of tenants
  - Likely cause: transit gateway route misconfiguration or security group block
  - Action: verify peering routes, check SG logs, verify DNS resolution from tenant subnets
- Symptom: High first-token latency after scale up
  - Likely cause: cold KV-cache on new nodes
  - Action: trigger cache-warmup job and monitor cache hit ratio
- Symptom: Intermittent model load failures
  - Likely cause: PV attach limits or kernel resource exhaustion
  - Action: check kubelet attach/detach logs, increase attach limit, or pre-warm PVs

Appendix A — cache-warmup job example (Kubernetes CronJob)
```
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: cache-warmup
  namespace: maintenance
spec:
  schedule: "@hourly"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: warmup
            image: internal-cli:stable
            env:
            - name: API_URL
              value: "https://internal-api.example.local"
            - name: API_KEY
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: internal-api-key
                  key: key
            command: ["/bin/sh","-c","/usr/local/bin/warmup /etc/warmup/prompts.txt"]
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```
